That, along with the numerous farmsteads and fence lines which helped break up the Southern formations, resulted in the repulse of both assaults.

claim: The post and rail fence along the Trostle-Wigert Lane, which Union forces used to reach battle sites from Taneytown Road, is documented in the 1872 survey and Tipton photographs
feature: Trostle-Wigert Lane fence (Trostle Field 10 south boundary)
quote: The Trostle-Wigert Lane was used by Union forces to reach battle sites and positions from Taneytown Road. This avenue of approach was a significant movement corridor for Union artillery and infantry throughout the last two days of the battle and was defended aggressively to prevent Confederate forces from attaining the Union rear. The fencing likely provided cover to Union forces traveling on the lane. Additionally the fence likely became an obstacle to lateral movement across the lane by both forces during the course of the battle.34 Post and rail fencing is documented in the 1872 topographical survey map and in photographs from the Tipton Collection

quote: The Snyder farmstead was incorporated into the Confederate battle line on Seminary Ridge and Confederate infantry and artillery occupied and fired from this site from July 2–4. Consequently, Union counter fire damaged the farmstead and Confederates used the buildings as emergency shelter.20 The orchard likely provided cover for Confederate troops and is documented in the 1863 Bachelder Map, 1863 Cope Map, 1863 Elliott Map, 1872 topographical survey map, and in photographs from the park’s historical collection (Figure 37).21 In 2007, the park completed replanting of the Snyder Orchard.
